Our Work · Voice Packs

The Voice Pack Archive

Before advocacy came vocabulary. Before vocabulary came understanding.

These four earlier editions of the Voice Pack are a record of how Aletheia’s thinking changed. Each one is a good resource in its own right. Read together, they show an organisation listening to young people, learning what they actually needed, and going back to make something better.

We started out thinking the problem was missing information. Young people kept showing us it was bigger than that: they needed words, then the confidence and know-how to use them, then a way to connect what was happening to them with what was happening to everyone else.

The question kept changing

Each edition asked a bigger question than the last

  1. Edition 01

    “What is happening in my body?”

    A reader finishes it thinking: “I understand my body.”

  2. Edition 02

    “How do I explain what I’m experiencing?”

    A reader finishes it thinking: “I understand what I’m experiencing, and can describe it.”

  3. Edition 03

    “What do I do when I’m not being heard?”

    A reader finishes it thinking: “I can navigate healthcare and advocate for myself.”

  4. Edition 04

    “How can young people change the systems affecting our health?”

    A reader finishes it thinking: “My experience connects to other young people’s, and our voices can influence systems.”

  5. Current

    “What do young people need to learn, speak, take part in and change their health, together?”

    Aletheia now builds the structures that make that possible.

Improvement through accumulation

Nothing was thrown away. Each edition added something.

The later packs didn’t replace body knowledge with advocacy. They kept every earlier idea and built on it. The current edition is different in one way: it connects them.

Edition 01knowledge=confidence in your body
Edition 02knowledge+language=confidence describing it
Edition 03knowledge+language+agency=self-advocacy
Edition 04knowledge+language+agency+collective voice=change
Current editionknowledge+language+agency+collective voice=integrated health agency

What each edition taught us

Learning, one edition at a time

After Edition 01

Knowledge removes shame

Plain, accurate information made bodies less embarrassing to talk about. But young people still froze when it came to explaining a symptom.

After Edition 02

Knowledge needs language

With the right words, young people described symptoms clearly. Many were still told it was normal.

After Edition 03

Language needs agency

Scripts, rights and pathways helped young people hold their ground. But each person was fighting the same fight alone.

After Edition 04

Agency needs collective voice

Shared experiences became evidence that could change schools, services and policy. The next step was bringing it all together.

One story, four editions

Why the model had to grow

Across the archive, a fictional young person called Maya has the same period pain. What changes is what each edition can do for her. Her story is the clearest way we know to explain why information on its own was never going to be enough.

  1. Edition 01

    Maya learns what period cramps are, and why they happen.

  2. Edition 02

    She tracks her pain: where it is, how long it lasts, how strong it is, what it stops.

  3. Edition 03

    She explains persistent pain to a clinician, is told it’s normal, and asks the questions that get her a referral.

  4. Edition 04

    She notices friends have similar stories, gathers them ethically through her SRC, and contributes to a youth consultation.

Current edition · April 2026

Heard. Understood. Me.

Everything the archive shows Aletheia learning, brought together. The current Voice Pack doesn’t treat knowledge, language, advocacy and change as separate stages. It treats them as one connected set of things young people can do, and lets you start wherever you are.

Read the current Voice Pack Open the PDF (opens in a new tab)

The archive documents the thinking behind today’s model. Aletheia began by trying to give young people better health information. Then we realised they needed words. Then that words needed to become agency. Then that individual agency operates inside systems. That’s how we became an organisation where young people aren’t just taught about health, but are equipped to navigate it, speak about it, advocate within it and help change it.
